Smith introduced Mandela to the London crowd gathered to celebrate his life with the words, “The one, the only, the birthday boy, Nelson Mandela, Nelson Mandelaaaaaaaaaa.”

London was the site of a concert 20 years earlier marking Mandela’s 70th birthday and raising awareness of his imprisonment.

“Your voices carried across the water to inspire us in our prison cells far away,” Mandela told cheering fans. “Tonight, we can stand before you free.

“But even as we celebrate, let us remind ourselves that our work is far from complete.

“Where there is poverty and sickness, including AIDS, where human beings are being oppressed, there is more work to be done. Our work is for freedom for all.”

As Mandela walked onto the stage, Smith led the crowd in a chorus of “Happy Birthday.”

Proceeds from the concert in London’s Hyde Park will go toward the 46664 Campaign, which Mandela founded in 2003 to raise awareness of the impact of AIDS, particularly in Africa, and to promote HIV-prevention measures worldwide. The charity’s name refers to Mandela’s prison number during his incarceration on Robben Island.

Organizers made 46,664 tickets available for the event.

The concert’s finale was scheduled to feature Queen, Amy Winehouse and Jerry Dammers performing “Free Nelson Mandela,” the 1980s hit by the Specials that quickly became an anti-apartheid anthem. In the end, however, nearly every act joined them on stage.

The former South African president turns 90 on July 18.

More than a dozen African artists, including Johnny Clegg and the Soweto Gospel Choir, also performed. Smith, music legend Quincy Jones and Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton were among the stars introducing acts.

Other guests at the concert included British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, former U.S. President Bill Clinton, talk show host Oprah Winfrey and actor Robert De Niro.

In 1964, a court sentenced Mandela to life in prison for plotting to overthrow the government through violence. He spent his first 18 years at Robben Island Prison, off Cape Town, South Africa, and later spent time at Pollsmoor Prison and Victor Verster Prison, closer to the mainland.

While imprisoned, Mandela came to be recognized as the most significant Black leader in South Africa and became a powerful symbol of resistance in the anti-apartheid movement. He consistently refused to compromise his political position in exchange for his freedom.

South African President F.W. de Klerk released Mandela in February 1990 after 27 years in prison. Mandela was elected president of the African National Congress the following year, and in 1994, he was elected president of South Africa.

On June 27, 2008, tens of thousands gathered in London’s Hyde Park for a star-filled tribute to the former South African president, anti-apartheid leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate, who had gone from prisoner number 46664 to one of the world’s most admired statesmen.

It was part of the 46664 campaign, Mandela’s global initiative to raise awareness about HIV/AIDS, named for the prison number he was assigned on Robben Island — prisoner 466 in the year 1964.

Mandela, then increasingly frail, appeared onstage to a thunderous ovation. Wearing one of his signature patterned shirts, he thanked the crowd and reminded them that the work of justice was not finished.

“Our work is for freedom for all,” Mandela told the audience, in what became one of his last major public appearances abroad.

The lineup reflected Mandela’s reach across generations and continents. Performers included Amy Winehouse, Annie Lennox, Queen + Paul Rodgers, Simple Minds, Leona Lewis, Sugababes, Razorlight, Joan Baez, Eddy Grant and South African artists including the Soweto Gospel Choir and Johnny Clegg. The concert also featured appearances by celebrity presenters and supporters, including Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith, Oprah Winfrey, former U.S. President Bill Clinton and other public figures who paid tribute to Mandela’s moral authority and political legacy.

One of the emotional centerpieces was “Free Nelson Mandela,” the 1984 protest anthem by The Special AKA, written by Jerry Dammers. The song had helped introduce Mandela’s name to a global pop audience during the years when he remained imprisoned under South Africa’s apartheid regime. At the birthday concert, its return served as both a reminder and a victory lap: a song once demanding Mandela’s release was now being performed in honor of his life’s triumph.

Mandela spent 27 years in prison for his role in the struggle against white minority rule in South Africa. He was arrested in 1962, sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964 during the Rivonia Trial and confined for much of his sentence on Robben Island. To apartheid authorities, he was inmate 46664. To millions around the world, he became the face of resistance.

Released in 1990, Mandela helped guide South Africa through negotiations that ended apartheid. In 1994, he became the country’s first Black president and its first democratically elected leader, ushering in a new era after decades of racial segregation and political repression.

The Hyde Park concert was not only a tribute to that journey but also a continuation of Mandela’s post-presidential mission. Through 46664, he pushed world leaders and ordinary citizens to confront HIV/AIDS, a crisis that devastated parts of Africa, including South Africa. Mandela spoke publicly and personally about the disease, especially after the death of his son Makgatho from AIDS-related complications in 2005.

For many in attendance, the 90th birthday concert captured the unusual arc of Mandela’s public life: from banned revolutionary to global elder statesman, from a man whose name could not be freely spoken in his own country to one celebrated by presidents, movie stars and musicians before a massive international audience.

The music carried the memory of protest. The celebrity tributes reflected his global stature. And the 46664 message underscored Mandela’s insistence that freedom was not a relic of the past, but a continuing obligation.

Mandela died in 2013 at age 95, but the Hyde Park celebration remains one of the defining public commemorations of his later years — a night when the world did not merely sing for Nelson Mandela, but sang back to a history he had helped change.
